overview: Holstein was a duchy south of the Eider, joined under the Danish king after a territorial settlement in 1773. Farms, the port towns of Kiel and Altona, a university and a new canal connected its inhabitants to a wider world. The imported record covers 1783 to 1878, but Holstein did not remain a separate duchy throughout that span: Prussia formally incorporated it in 1867 after the wars of 1864 and 1866.

periods.summary: Agricultural reforms, canal traffic and growing towns changed life under the Danish crown.

periods.title: War and annexation
periods.summary: The wars of 1864 and 1866 ended in incorporation into Prussia in January 1867.

sections.title: A duchy, its people and a promise of freedom

items.text: A ceremony at Kiel Castle on 16 November 1773 made a major territorial settlement tangible. The representative of the Gottorf side handed over a key, a piece of turf and a green twig to the Danish king’s representative. These objects stood for the territory being transferred. A diplomatic agreement could arrive with a small piece of lawn.

Salons in Kiel and Altona became places to read, discuss ideas, drink tea or coffee and smoke. Their participants questioned old privileges and debated how society should work. This educated circle was only a small minority of the population, but its conversations helped spread the ideas behind agricultural reform.

Writing sample: a December 1804 ordinance proclaimed, “Die Leibeigenschaft ist in Unsern Herzogtümern Schleswig und Holstein, von dem 1sten Januar 1805 an, gänzlich und auf immer abgeschafft,” meaning “Serfdom in our duchies Schleswig and Holstein is completely and forever abolished from 1 January 1805.” This German text follows the historical society’s transcription of the ordinance.

Personal freedom did not automatically provide land or a secure income. Former serfs could become wage laborers or face expensive rents, while landlords shed older obligations to support dependents. The reform changed legal status decisively, but many households still had to struggle for food, work and a place to live.

The canal built from 1777 to 1784 joined Kiel’s Baltic inlet to the Eider river route toward the North Sea. Six locks helped ships negotiate changing water levels. Warehouses at Holtenau, Rendsburg and Tönning stored and transferred cargo. Holtenau’s surviving warehouse was built while the canal itself was still under construction.

At Landwehr, the new canal cut across an existing road, so builders provided a Dutch-style drawbridge. A horse station stood nearby. Horses walking on the towpath pulled ships through the canal: part of a vessel’s journey could depend on legs moving along the bank rather than sails moving above the water.

The Altona to Kiel railway crossed difficult ground, including marshes and hills. Its construction required 333 bridges and culverts, the passages carrying water beneath the track. Regular trains began running on 9 September 1844, before the official opening ceremony on 18 September. Grand celebrations and the working timetable were separate events.

Kiel’s university had been founded in 1665, long before this map record begins. Professors and students enjoyed special privileges, including their own legal jurisdiction and exemption from certain taxes. These arrangements lasted into the nineteenth century and ended under Prussian rule in 1867. Being a university member could change which authorities dealt with you.

In 1802 the university took over Georg Heinrich Weber’s private clinic. The resulting academic hospital linked treatment with teaching and research at patients’ bedsides. Medical students could learn from actual illness as well as lectures. The institution helped connect university study with the urgent practical needs of people who were sick.

Kiel’s older water pipes included hollowed tree trunks joined together. An 1821 bequest helped replace wooden pipes in Holstenstraße with iron ones. Most residents collected water in containers from public outlets; wealthier households could pay for private connections. Carrying the day’s water was a regular household task, not a turn of a kitchen tap.

Wells were not automatically a clean alternative. Kiel’s archive history describes pollution from nearby latrines and leaking waste. In a crowded town, the places where people disposed of waste and obtained drinking water could sit dangerously close together. Water supply and toilets were parts of the same public-health problem.

In 1862 the king transferred the Schreventeich pond to Kiel, and new waterworks followed in 1863. They supplied untreated, unfiltered surface water. Piped delivery was convenient, but the technology did not yet guarantee clean drinking water. Some residents continued to prefer water from street pumps.

After annexation, Prussian officials celebrated at Kiel Castle on 24 January 1867 with bells and salutes. Many local people had instead hoped for their own duke, Friedrich VIII. The new three-year military-service requirement also mattered to families; the state archive exhibition records young men emigrating to escape it.

ending.text: Following the wars of 1864 and 1866, a patent of 12 January 1867 incorporated Schleswig-Holstein into Prussia. New provincial and district institutions replaced the earlier administration. The map’s continuation to 1878 therefore includes years under Prussian rule, rather than eleven additional years of a separate Holstein duchy.
